body.p: This Amendment is responsive to the Office Action dated December 6, 2022. Applicant has amended claims 1, 5, 10, 14, 18, and 20. Claims 1-20 are pending upon entry of this communication.
In a telephonic interview on February 9, 2023, Applicant's representative, Ambar P.

Nayate (Reg. No. 65,393), and Examiners Wallace and Jenness discussed the present matter. Inparticular, Mr. Nayate and Examiners Wallace and Jenness discussed amendments to the independent claims to advance prosecution. Examiners Wallace and Jenness agreed that the rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 101 of claim 1 for reciting transitory media should be withdrawn without reciting "non-transitory."
No agreement was reached as to allowability. No demonstrations were made, and no exhibits were presented. Applicant thanks Examiners Wallace and Jenness for the interview.

The Office Action rejected claims 1-20 under 35 U.S.C. § 101 based on an assertion that these claims are directed to non-statutory subject matter. Although Applicant does not agree to the rejection, Applicant has amended independent claims 1, 10, and 18 as discussed during the interview to overcome the rejection. For instance, the amended independent claims recite "causing delivery of insulin to the patient, with an insulin delivery device, based on generating an output indicative of the amount of insulin to counteract the glucose level increase caused by consumption of the meal," which was discussed to overcome the rejection. Applicant respectfully requests withdrawal of the rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 101 of claims 1-20.
The Office Action rejected claims 1-3, 5-12, and 14-20 under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1) as being anticipated by U.S. Publication No. 2007/0179434 Al by Weinert (hereinafter, "Weinert").

Without conceding the merits of the rejection, Applicant has amended the claims solely to expedite prosecution towards allowance. Applicant respectfully traverses the rejections to the extent the rejections may be considered applicable to the amended claims. Weinert fails to
disclose all of the features of the amended claims, as required by 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1), and provides no apparent reason for modification to include such features.
Independent claim 1
Amended claim 1 recites, with emphasis:
A system comprising:
one or more processors; and
one or more processor-readable storage media storing instructions which, when

executed by the one or more processors, cause performance of: obtaining an estimated protein value for a meal; determining an equivalent carbohydrate value for the meal based on converting the estimated protein value into a corresponding carbohydrate
determining, based on the equivalent carbohydrate value for the meal, an amount of insulin to deliver to a patient to counteract a glucose level increase
caused by consumption of the meal; and
causing delivery of insulin to the patient, with an insulin delivery device, based on generating an output indicative of the amount of insulin to counteract the
glucose level increase caused by consumption of the meal.

As emphasized, amended claim 1 clarifies "determining an equivalent carbohydrate value for the meal based on converting the estimated protein value into a corresponding carbohydrate value." Weinert fails to disclose or suggest any conversion of estimated protein value into a corresponding carbohydrate value.

In support of the rejection, the Office Action cited paragraph [0010] of Weinert which states "[t]he processor may be configured to control the display unit to display the values of the expected speed in the form of a fat amount, a protein amount and a carbohydrate amount, and to display the values of the carbohydrate content in the form of meal size values for each of the fat amount, protein amount and carbohydrate amount."
To the extent that paragraph [0010] of Weinert states "display[ing] the values of the

carbohydrate content in the form of meal size values of each of the fat amount, protein amount and carbohydrate amount," nothing in such disclosure relates to "converting the estimated protein value into a corresponding carbohydrate value," as set forth in amended claim 1. Any reading of paragraph [0010] of Weinert that displaying the values of carbohydrate content includes converting estimated protein value into a corresponding carbohydrate value is not supported by the language of paragraph [0010] of Weinert or other portions of Weinert.

Indeed, in paragraph [0010] itself, Weinert describes "carbohydrate content" as being "in the form of meal size values," and not any conversion of protein value. In fact, the description in paragraph [0010] of Weinert is for a way to display for receiving user input. For instance, paragraph [0010] of Weinert states that "[t]he processor may be configured to control the display unit to display a graphical user interface having a first axis defined by values of the carbohydrate content and a second axis defined by values of the expected speed of overall glucose absorption from the meal by the user," and "[t]he graphical user interface may provide for the user input of feed forward information in the form of user selection of corresponding pairs of the carbohydrate content and expected speed values" (emphasis added).

Clearly, the cited portions of Weinert are related to how a user can input information about meal size, which Weinert describes as being "carbohydrate content." It is in this context, of user input, that paragraph [0010] of Weinert should be considered. However, nothing in the user input about meal size involves "determining an equivalent carbohydrate value for the meal based on converting the estimated protein value into a corresponding carbohydrate value" (emphasis added), as set forth in amended claim 1.

As further evidence, paragraph [0079] of Weinert states that "[r]eferring to FIG. 2, one exemplary embodiment of such a graphical user interface 50 providing for user input of meal intake information is shown," and "[i]n the illustrated embodiment, the graphical user interface 50 is a grid-type user interface having one grid axis defined by carbohydrate content in the form of meal size and another grid axis defined by expected speed of overall glucose absorption from the meal by the patient in the form of meal duration." FIG. 2 is reproduced below.
FIG. 2
Again, Weinert is describing user input for meal size, which is considered as
carbohydrate content, but provides no disclosure of any conversion of protein value to a corresponding carbohydrate value.

As even more evidence, in paragraph [0081], Weinert states that "[r]eferring to FIG. 4, yet another exemplary embodiment of a graphical user interface 54 providing for user input of meal intake information is shown," and "[i]n the illustrated embodiment, the graphical user interface 54 is a grid-type user interface having one grid axis defined by carbohydrate content in the form of meal size and another grid axis defined by expected speed of overall glucose absorption in the form of fat amount, protein amount and carbohydrate amount of the meal" (emphasis added). FIG. 4 is reproduced below.
FIG. 4
The example of FIG. 4 in Weinert illustrates user input of fat amount, protein amount,

and carbohydrate amount. However, nothing in such user input involves any determination of an equivalent carbohydrate value for the meal based on converting the estimated protein value into a corresponding carbohydrate value, as set forth in amended claim 1.

For at least these reasons, Weinert fails to disclose or suggest the features of amended claim 1. Weinert fails to disclose or suggest the features of amended claims 10 and 18 at least for similar reasons discussed with respect to claim 1. The dependent claims recite novel and
non-obvious features by virtue of dependency upon respective independent claims, but may recite novel and non-obvious features for additional reasons as well.
For example, dependent claims 5 and 14 recite additional features that Weinert fails to

disclose or suggest. For instance, claim 5 recites "determining a conversion factor for converting protein to a parameter approximating an effect of the protein on glucose levels of the patient," and "determining the equivalent carbohydrate for the meal based on converting the estimated protein value for the meal into the corresponding carbohydrate value using the conversion factor." Claim 14 recites similar features.
Weinert does not disclose any conversion factor for converting protein to a parameter

approximating an effect of the protein on glucose levels of the patient. Rather, similar to above, the cited portions of Weinert for allegedly disclosing the features of claims 5 and 14 relate to user input, and no conversion factor. For instance, for claims 5 and 14, the Office Action cited paragraphs [0081] and [0083]. As noted above, paragraph [0081] relates to the user input of FIG. 4. For paragraph [0083], Weinert states that "[r]eferring to FIG. 5, still another exemplary embodiment of a graphical user interface 56 providing for user input of meal intake information is shown" (emphasis added). Like above, Weinert is describing user input, and provides no disclosure related to "determining a conversion factor for converting protein to a parameter approximating an effect of the protein on glucose levels of the patient," much less "determining the equivalent carbohydrate for the meal based on converting the estimated protein value for the meal into the corresponding carbohydrate value using the conversion factor," as set forth in claim 5, and similar features of claim 14.
For at least these additional reasons, Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration and withdrawal of the rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1) of claims 1-3, 5-12, and 14-20.
The Office Action rejected claims 4 and 13 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over Weinert in view of U.S. Publication No. 2018/0200439 Al by Mazlish (hereinafter, "Mazlish").
Applicant respectfully traverses the rejections. The applied references, alone or in any combination, fail to disclose or suggest the features defined by the claims, and there would have
been no apparent reason that would have caused one of ordinary skill in the art to modify the techniques of the applied references to arrive at the claimed features.
Claims 4 and 13 are allowable at least by virtue of dependency upon respective

independent claims 1 and 10, but may be allowable for additional reasons as well. Mazlish fails to provide additional disclosure to overcome the deficiencies of Weinert described above. Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration and withdrawal of the rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 103.

Applicant does not concede that the subject matter encompassed by the claims prior to this Response is unpatentable over the art cited by the Office Action. While several distinctions have been noted over the art of record, Applicant notes that there may be several other limitations that are neither taught nor suggested by the art of record. Applicant expressly reserves all rights and arguments with respect to distinctions not explicitly noted herein. In addition, to the extent that amendments included herein constitute a narrowing of the claims, such narrowing of the claims should not be construed as an admission as to the merits of the prior rejections. Indeed, Applicant traverses the rejections and preserves all rights and arguments. To the extent that any particular statement or argument by the Office in the pending Office Action has not been explicitly addressed herein, the same should not be construed as an acquiescence or admission by the Applicant that such statements or arguments by the Office are accurate and proper.
